extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, literary students and scholars (readers of classical poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetic imitation (especially tragedy and epic) covering plot, diction, metre, and poetic licenses; aimed at helping poets/dramaturgs craft unified, effective works. Drawn from classical poetics with examples and anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style
rubrics_metrics.description: “The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear diction should avoid meanness; balance clarity with elevation. Use current/proper words for perspicuity but avoid making the style mean or commonplace. The clearest style is that which uses only current or proper words; yet this can be mean (illustrated by the poetry of Cleophon and Sthenelus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of current/proper words for clearness
rubrics_metrics.description: “The clearest style is that which uses only current or proper words.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer ordinary, current vocabulary when the goal is perspicuity (especially where speech is to resemble common usage). Overuse of unusual terms reduces clarity; current words make diction perspicuous and intelligible to hearers/readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lofty style uses unusual words and ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Lofty style is raised above the commonplace by employing unusual (strange or rare) words, metaphorical language, lengthened forms, and other ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unusual words and metaphors raise diction above commonness; they provide distinction and loftiness. However, a style wholly composed of such elements becomes either a riddle (if metaphorical) or a jargon (if composed of strange/rare words). Use these elements sparingly to elevate without obscuring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in licenses of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Any license of speech (metaphor, strange words, lengthening, contraction, alteration) must be used with moderation; obtrusive employment is grotesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive or obtrusive use produces ludicrous effect. Critics who censure these licenses indiscriminately err; the licenses give distinction when used properly but are grotesque if overused. Example: Eucleides’ caricature demonstrates how abuse makes poetry trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-formation licenses (lengthening/contraction/alteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: A word is lengthened when a vowel is made longer or a syllable is inserted; contracted when part is removed; altered when part remains and part is re-cast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lengthening, contraction, and alteration create distinction while retaining partial conformity with usage to preserve perspicuity. These devices contribute to clearness remote from commonness and are defended against critics when used appropriately (examples of forms are given in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate vs grotesque application of word-licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: To employ such licenses obtrusively is grotesque; they must be applied with propriety and moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even valuable devices (lengthening, rare words, metaphors) become ludicrous if used solely to attract attention. Use them where they enhance effect (e.g., inserting ordinary forms in epic verse) rather than for mere novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety in use of compound and rare words
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe propriety in compound words, strange (or rare) words, and other modes of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such forms give distinction to style precisely because they differ from current idiom (examples of phrases ridiculed by contemporaries are cited). But propriety requires selecting them where fitting and not as forced affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor as the highest poetic skill
rubrics_metrics.description: “But the greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor. This alone cannot be imparted by another; it is the mark of genius.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor requires an eye for resemblances; it is central to poetic excellence. It distinguishes great poets and is especially appropriate for certain meters (notably iambic). It cannot be taught like a technical rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate lexical varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of the various kinds of words, the compound are best adapted to dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, metaphors to iambic. In heroic poetry, indeed, all these varieties are serviceable. But in iambic verse ... the most appropriate words are those which are found even in prose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose word-types according to genre and metre: dithyrambs suit compounds, heroic (epic) poetry tolerates/benefits from rare words and metaphors, iambic should approximate familiar speech (current/proper words plus measured ornament).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (tragedy and dramatic imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot ought, as in a tragedy, to be constructed on dramatic principles: it should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single, coherent action produces the appropriate pleasure of imitation; avoid attempting to cover an excessively vast subject (e.g., the whole Trojan War). Break larger subjects into single portions or episodes to preserve unity and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative imitation follows dramatic principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative poetic imitation in a single metre should, manifestly, be constructed on dramatic principles and have a single action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in epic/narrative forms, the unity of action should be maintained (the poem should resemble a single and coherent picture). Historical compositions differ because they present a period rather than a single action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrational elements within the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything irrational should, if possible, be excluded; or at all events it should lie outside the action of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrational incidents within the dramatic action undermine credibility (examples: messenger’s implausible accounts, mute characters arriving improbably). If irrationality is included, it must be rendered plausible or placed outside the play’s central action (e.g., hero’s ignorance about a fact may lie outside the action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable possibilities to improbable ones
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should prefer probable possibilities to improbable possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select events that the audience can accept as likely; the plot must not be composed of irrational parts. If an improbable event is necessary, it must be presented so that an air of likelihood is imparted (poetic charm may veil absurdity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should speak as little as possible in own person
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person, for it is not this that makes him an imitator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit authorial intrusion; allow characters and action to perform the imitation. Other poets who appear frequently in their works imitate less effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy: scale and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry differs from Tragedy in the scale on which it is constructed, and in its metre. The heroic measure has proved its fitness by the test of experience ... it most readily admits rare words and metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heroic (epic) metre for large-scale narrative; heroic metre suits stately diction, rare words and metaphors. Mixing different metres is incongruous and to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic’s capacity for simultaneity and episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: In Epic poetry, owing to the narrative form, many events simultaneously transacted can be presented; episodes, if relevant, add mass and dignity and relieve sameness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic may include simultaneous actions and multiple episodes to enrich the poem, provided they contribute to the subject and do not undermine unity of action. This is an advantage over stage-bound tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metre selection by nature and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature herself teaches the choice of the proper measure: heroic for narrative; iambic and trochaic tetrameter for stirring/dance-like measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select metre to suit both content and effect. Trochaic tetrameter is akin to dancing; iambic expresses action. Avoid mixing metres in one large-scale composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction elaborated in pauses; avoid over-brilliance amid character/thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought. Conversely, character and thought are merely obscured by a diction that is over brilliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate diction for moments without character expression; when character or thought is being expressed, use clarity to prevent obscuring them. Over-elaboration during active expression weakens characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish essential vs accidental faults in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the art of poetry there are two kinds of faults—those which touch its essence, and those which are accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors of imitation (essential faults) are more serious (e.g., inability to imitate correctly). Accidental faults (e.g., minor technical inaccuracies from other arts) are less serious, though still to be avoided when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors may be justified if they attain the end of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: If a poet describes the impossible, he is guilty of an error; but the error may be justified, if the end of the art be thereby attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An artistic breach of fact can be tolerated when it produces the intended poetic effect (e.g., the pursuit of Hector). But if the same end could be reached without violating rules, the violation is unjustified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual evaluation of actions/words
rubrics_metrics.description: In examining whether what has been said or done by some one is poetically right or not, we must consider by whom it is said or done, to whom, when, in whose interest, or for what end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lines and actions with attention to speaker, audience, timing, and purpose. A speech that is unacceptable in one context may be justified in another if it secures a greater good or fits a dramatic aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the wonderful and the irrational—pleasing but to be veiled
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful is admitted in Tragedy ... The wonderful is pleasing ... The secret lies in a fallacy: men infer the first from the second; therefore a false first may be tolerated if the second is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ marvels or improbable elements sparingly and mask their absurdity with convincing particulars. The audience’s tendency to infer justifies certain fictional liberties when they support the dramatic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose single hero/period/action to avoid over-complication
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a single hero, a single period, or a single action; attempting to embrace too much makes the subject over-complicated and not easily embraced in a single view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For dramatic effectiveness, keep scope moderate — detach portions as separate subjects or use episodes sparingly. Large epics can be composed of many such moderate units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts required in epic/tragedy (reversals, recognitions, tragic incidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts also, with the exception of song and scenery, are the same [in epic and tragedy]; for it requires reversals of intention, recognitions, and tragic incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots with the dramatic mechanisms (peripeteia, anagnorisis, catastrophe) to achieve the intended emotional effects. Song and scenery are adjuncts and treated differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vehicle of expression: varieties of language allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: The vehicle of expression is language—either current terms or, it may be, rare words or metaphors. There are also many modifications of language which we concede to the poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept a range of linguistic choices for poetic purposes; poetic correctness differs from that in other arts (such as politics). Choose among current words, rare words, metaphors, and modifications depending on effect and genre.
